aliases.name: Gelloudes
aliases.meaning: plural form denoting a class of demons

aliases.name: Abyzou
aliases.meaning: from abyssos, 'the deep'; identified with Gello in late antiquity and Byzantine literature

description.summary: A female demon of Greek and Byzantine tradition, attested as early as Sappho (6th century BC), said to attack pregnant women, newborns, and the unmarried, and the central target of a long-running corpus of apotropaic charms and exorcisms in the Greek-speaking world.
description.full: Gello (Greek: Γελλώ; later plural Gelloudes, γελοῦδες) is a female demon attested in Greek literature from the archaic period through the Byzantine and modern Greek folk traditions. Earliest references are in a fragment attributed to Sappho (6th century BC) and in later proverb-collections (Zenobius, 2nd century AD; Hesychius, 5th–6th century), where Gello is said to be the ghost (eidolon) of a young woman who died unwed or childless and returns to harm pregnant women, infants, and virgins. In the Byzantine period the singular figure became a class of beings; John of Damascus (8th century) equated the gelloudes with stryngai (witches who fly at night and strangle children), and Michael Psellos (11th century) wrote a treatise discussing their nature and proposing a connection with the Hebrew Lilith. The 'Legend of Saint Sisinnios' — preserved in Greek, Coptic, Ethiopic, Slavonic, Romanian, and other manuscripts — narrates how the saint pursues Gyllou after she kills the children of Melitene, forcing her to reveal her many secret names so they may be inscribed on protective amulets. The tradition lies behind a vast corpus of Byzantine apotropaic amulets (often invoking Sisinnios or Solomon as a 'holy rider' spearing the demon), exorcisms, and folk practices that remained in use into the 20th century.

etymology.origin: The name Gello has been linked by Carl Frank, Walter Burkert, and M. L. West to the Akkadian/Mesopotamian demon Gallû, a class of underworld spirits associated with sickness and death; this same root has also been argued to underlie the later Arabic/English 'ghoul'. A Greek folk-etymology connected the name to gel- ('grin, laugh').
etymology.meaning: In its earliest Greek attestations, Gello is the unappeased ghost of a young woman dead before her time. The plural gelloudes designates child-killing female demons.
etymology.first_use: Attested in a fragment of Sappho (6th century BC); the plural gelloudes is first found in John of Damascus (8th century AD).

related_phenomena.name: Lamia
related_phenomena.description: Greek child-killing female demon often paired with Gello in classical sources

related_phenomena.name: Strzyga / Stryngai
related_phenomena.description: Slavic and Byzantine night-flying witch demons equated with the gelloudes by John of Damascus

related_phenomena.name: Night Hag (Lilith and analogues)
related_phenomena.description: Pan-Mediterranean and Near Eastern child-killing female demon tradition; explicitly compared to Gello by Michael Psellos

related_phenomena.name: Ghul
related_phenomena.description: Possibly cognate via a shared Mesopotamian Gallû etymology (Frank, Burkert, West)

related_phenomena.name: Empusa
related_phenomena.description: Greek shape-shifting female demon often grouped with Lamia and Gello

coloration: unspecified; described as appearing in human or monstrous form

features.description: Often appears as a young woman or, in later Byzantine tradition, as an old crone or witch
Said to take the form of a fly, snake, dragon, or reptile in order to enter sealed rooms
Depicted on Byzantine amulets with a fish- or serpent-tailed lower body
Possesses 'twelve and a half' secret names that, when written on an amulet, force her to depart (Legend of Saint Sisinnios)

physical.morphology: In classical sources Gello is the bodiless ghost (eidolon) of a young woman; in Byzantine sources she is a flying, shape-shifting demon, sometimes depicted on amulets with a fish- or serpent-like lower body. Orthodox theology of the period officially denied she could possess a real body.

abilities.description: Strangles newborns or carries them off; said to attack children before baptism in particular
Attacks pregnant women, causing miscarriage or stillbirth
Said to render nursing mothers unable to feed their infants
Transforms into a fly or other small creature to slip through closed doors and windows
Forced to reveal her names and depart when confronted by Saint Sisinnios or the archangel Michael

habitat_preference: domestic spaces, especially nurseries and lying-in chambers
behavior.diet: Said to drink the blood and devour the vital fluids of infants
patterns: Targets pregnant women, women in childbirth, and unbaptized infants
Most active at night, in the days between birth and baptism
Repelled by Christian symbols, baptism, naming exorcisms, and inscribed amulets

range.description: Originally a localized Greek tradition (attested for Sappho on Lesbos), the Gello / gelloudes complex spread throughout the Greek-speaking Byzantine world and, through the 'Legend of Saint Sisinnios', into Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Romanian, Slavonic, Arabic, Syriac, and Hebrew manuscript traditions across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East.

hotspots.name: Lesbos

location.description: Island of Lesbos, eastern Aegean — home of Sappho, the earliest source for Gello

hotspots.notes: Earliest attested context for Gello, in a fragment of Sappho preserved by Zenobius

hotspots.name: Constantinople

location.description: Imperial capital of the Byzantine Empire; centre of the gelloudes literature, exorcisms, and amulet production

hotspots.notes: Setting of the 'Legend of Saint Sisinnios' (in some versions, Melitene's tower stands at Chalcopratia in Constantinople)

first_recorded.source: Sappho fragment (6th century BC), preserved in later proverb collections

peak_activity_periods.description: Byzantine era: codification of the gelloudes tradition by John of Damascus, Michael Psellos, and Nikephoros Kallistos Xanthopoulos; production of Sisinnios amulets
Manuscript proliferation of the Legend of Saint Sisinnios; documentation by Leo Allatios

temporal.seasonal_patterns: No specific seasonal pattern documented; risk concentrated in the period between birth and baptism.

origins.cultural_roots: Ancient Greek (archaic Aegean) tradition, with possible roots in Mesopotamian (Akkadian Gallû) demonology. Gello is best understood as part of a Mediterranean and Near Eastern complex of female reproductive demons that includes Lamia, Mormo, Empusa, Lilith, and Abyzou.
origins.earliest_accounts: A fragment attributed to Sappho (6th century BC) refers to Gello as a notorious threat to children; this fragment is preserved by the proverb-collector Zenobius (2nd century AD) and the lexicographer Hesychius of Alexandria (5th–6th century).
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to Lamia, Mormo, and Empusa in classical Greek tradition; equated with stryngai (witches) by John of Damascus; compared to Lilith by Michael Psellos; equated with Abyzou (the strangler of newborns from the Testament of Solomon) on Byzantine amulets.

timeline.event: Sappho refers to Gello as more devoted to children than even Gello herself, in a fragment preserved by Zenobius
timeline.significance: Earliest attestation of Gello in Greek literature

timeline.event: Zenobius compiles the proverb 'fonder of children than Gello' with explanatory notes
timeline.significance: First explicit etiology: Gello as the ghost of a young woman who died before her time

timeline.event: John of Damascus discusses gelloudes (plural) as nocturnal child-killing witches synonymous with stryngai
timeline.significance: Earliest plural usage; bridges classical demonology and Byzantine folk-Christianity
timeline.source: John of Damascus, attributed treatises on demons

timeline.event: Michael Psellos writes a treatise on the gelloudes, discussing their attacks on pregnant women and infants and proposing a connection to Hebrew Lilith
timeline.source: Michael Psellos, Peri Energeias Daimonon and related works

timeline.event: Nikephoros Kallistos Xanthopoulos describes gelloudes removing infants from their bedrooms
timeline.significance: Continued ecclesiastical engagement with the tradition

timeline.event: Earliest surviving manuscript of the 'Legend of Saint Sisinnios', in which Gyllou kills the children of Melitene and is forced to reveal her secret names
timeline.significance: Foundational legend behind the Byzantine and post-Byzantine apotropaic amulet tradition

timeline.event: Leo Allatios publishes 'De Graecorum hodie quorundam opinionibus', collecting contemporary Greek beliefs about Gello and other demons and criticizing certain folk practices
timeline.source: Leo Allatios, De Graecorum hodie quorundam opinionibus (Cologne, 1645)

history.modern_era: Modern Greek folklore has continued to invoke Gyllou and Baskania (the evil eye) in apotropaic prayers and exorcisms into the 20th century. Scholarly attention from Sarah Iles Johnston, Karen Hartnup, Richard P. H. Greenfield, and Jeffrey Spier has reframed Gello as a key node in Mediterranean demonology and the history of the apotropaic amulet.

physical.name: Byzantine 'holy rider' amulets
physical.description: Bronze and silver amulets, mostly 6th–13th century, depicting a mounted saint (Sisinnios or Solomon) spearing a female demon labelled Abyzou or Gyllou, with apotropaic inscriptions invoking Christ, Mary, and named saints.
physical.analysis: Catalogued by Jeffrey Spier in 'Medieval Byzantine Magical Amulets and Their Tradition' (Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes, 1993).

documentary.name: Legend of Saint Sisinnios
documentary.description: A multilingual manuscript tradition (Greek, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Romanian, Slavonic, Arabic, Syriac, Hebrew) narrating Gyllou's killing of the children of Melitene and her forced revelation of her secret names.
documentary.analysis: The standard scholarly survey is Richard P. H. Greenfield, 'Saint Sisinnios, the Archangel Michael and the Female Demon Gylou' (1989).

documentary.name: De Graecorum hodie quorundam opinionibus
documentary.description: Leo Allatios's Latin treatise on 17th-century Greek folk beliefs, including extended treatment of Gello and the gelloudes.
documentary.analysis: Reissued and analysed in Karen Hartnup, 'On the Beliefs of the Greeks' (Brill, 2004).

paranormal.name: Restless ghost / unappeased dead
paranormal.description: Classical interpretation: Gello is the ghost (eidolon) of a young woman who died before her time and unwed, whose bitterness or unfulfilled life makes her dangerous to children and pregnant women.
evidence_cited: The Sapphic fragment as preserved by Zenobius

paranormal.name: Demonic / Satanic witch tradition
paranormal.description: Byzantine Christian interpretation: Gello (as the gelloudes) is a class of demons, identified with the stryngai of pagan tradition and ultimately with the Devil's agents; certain women may be accused of becoming gelloudes through diabolical pact.
evidence_cited: Patristic and Byzantine treatises on demons
Trial records (e.g. Life of Tarasius, 9th century)

skeptical.name: Folkloric explanation for infant mortality
skeptical.description: Modern scholarship treats Gello as a personification of pre-modern infant mortality, miscarriage, sudden infant death, and puerperal complications, providing a culturally meaningful narrative for losses with otherwise opaque causes.
evidence_cited: Concentration of Gello-attacks in the period before baptism, when historical infant mortality was highest
Continuity of the tradition with other Mediterranean child-killing demon types (Lamia, Lilith, Abyzou)

skeptical.name: Diffusionist / Mesopotamian origin
skeptical.description: The name and figure are argued to derive from the Akkadian Gallû, an underworld demon; Gello is then one node in a wider Mediterranean and Near Eastern reproductive-demon complex.
evidence_cited: Shared functional profile across Mesopotamian, Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic traditions

traditions: Greek and Byzantine apotropaic amulets invoking Saint Sisinnios or Solomon
Greek folk exorcisms naming Gello/Gyllou and her many secret names
Use of red coral, garlic, and Christian symbols at the cradle in modern Greek folk practice
stories: Sappho's fragment on Gello (6th century BC, via Zenobius)
The Legend of Saint Sisinnios and the demon Gyllou (15th century manuscript)
Leo Allatios's accounts of 17th-century Greek belief in elderly women becoming gelloudes
folklore.beliefs: In Greek and Byzantine tradition, Gello and her plural gelloudes embody the dangers facing pregnant women, women in childbed, and unbaptized infants. Protection is sought through Christian rite (especially baptism), inscribed amulets bearing the saint's image and the demon's secret names, and named exorcism.

literature: Sarah Iles Johnston, 'Restless Dead: Encounters Between the Living and the Dead in Ancient Greece' (1999)
Karen Hartnup, 'On the Beliefs of the Greeks: Leo Allatios and Popular Orthodoxy' (Brill, 2004)
other: Modern Greek folk apotropaic prayers against Baskania (the evil eye), in continuity with the Gello tradition

researchers.name: Sarah Iles Johnston
researchers.contribution: Comprehensive analysis of Greek demonic and ghost traditions, including Gello, in 'Restless Dead' (1999)

researchers.name: Richard P. H. Greenfield
researchers.contribution: Standard scholarly study of Saint Sisinnios and the female demon Gylou (1989)

researchers.name: Jeffrey Spier
researchers.contribution: Catalogue and analysis of Byzantine apotropaic amulets, including Gello/Abyzou types (1993)

researchers.name: Karen Hartnup
researchers.contribution: Monograph on Leo Allatios and 17th-century Greek demonology (Brill, 2004)

researchers.name: Leo Allatios (Allatius)
researchers.contribution: First major Western scholarly survey of contemporary Greek beliefs about Gello and the gelloudes (1645)

research.ongoing_studies: Ongoing work in Byzantine demonology and the comparative study of Mediterranean and Near Eastern child-killing demon traditions (Gello, Lilith, Abyzou, Lamia).
